{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Jerome Paul Levine''' (May 4, 1937 – April 8, 2006) was a [[mathematician]] who contributed to the understanding of [[knot theory]].

==Education and career==

Born in [[New York City]], Levine received his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1958, and his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in [[mathematics]] from [[Princeton University]] in 1962, studying under [[Norman Steenrod]]. He began his career as an instructor at M.I.T., after which he spent a year at the [[University of Cambridge]] under a [[National Science Foundation]] [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral]] [[fellow]]ship. He became a professor at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1964, and in 1966 he left for [[Brandeis University]]. His early work helped to develop [[surgery theory]] as a powerful tool in knot theory and in [[geometric topology]]. In 1970 he was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Nice.<ref>{{cite book|author=Levine, J.|chapter=The role of the Seifert matrix in knot theory|title=Actes du Congrès international des mathématiciens, 1–10 Septembre 1970, Nice|year=1971|volume=Tome 2|pages=95–98}}</ref>

Jerome Levine died after a long and hard-fought battle with [[lymphatic cancer]] at the age of 68. He was an active mathematician at Brandeis until his death, with his last paper<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Levine |first=Jerome |date=2006-08-09 |title=Labeled binary planar trees and quasi-Lie algebras |journal=[[Algebraic & Geometric Topology]]  |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=935–948 |doi=10.2140/agt.2006.6.935|arxiv=math/0504278 }}</ref> published four months after he died.
